title: Error Handling
description: Learn why error handling is essential for building reliable applications, how C# exceptions work, and the strategies for gracefully recovering from errors without crashing.

data.text: Every real-world application will eventually encounter something it didn't expect: a missing file, an invalid network response, a database timeout, or even a simple typo in user input. **Error handling** is the practice of anticipating these failures and responding to them gracefully, rather than letting the application crash or behave unpredictably.

An **exception** is an object created by the .NET runtime when something goes wrong during program execution. It carries information about the problem — a human-readable message, a stack trace showing where the error originated, and sometimes an inner exception with additional context.

When an exception is thrown and no code catches it, the application terminates. In a command-line tool this might just mean an ugly stack trace in the console. In a web application or desktop app, it can mean data loss, corrupted state, or a complete shutdown for the user.

data.title: Key Principle
data.text: Never let exceptions go unhandled in production code. A well-written application anticipates problems and handles them explicitly — logging the error, showing a meaningful message to the user, and attempting recovery where possible.
What Happens When an Error Occurs?

When the .NET runtime encounters a problem, it creates an exception object and then searches backward through the call stack looking for a matching `catch` block. If none is found, the program terminates. This search process is called **exception propagation** or **bubbling up**.

data.caption: How an exception bubbles up the call stack when no catch block is found
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Method A calls B] --> B[Method B calls C]
    B --> C[Method C throws DivideByZeroException]
    C --> D{Does Method B have catch?}
    D -->|No| E[Bubbles up to Method A]
    D -->|Yes| F[Handled by Method B]
    E --> G{Does Method A have catch?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Handled by Method A]
    G -->|No| I[Unhandled - app crashes]

data.text: Common Things That Can Go Wrong

Errors in C# applications come from many sources. Some are caused by bugs in your own code, while others are caused by external factors you cannot fully control. Recognizing these categories helps you decide where to place error-handling logic.

rows: Using a variable that is null
Accessing an index that does not exist

data.title: Benefits of Error Handling
items: Prevents application crashes that inconvenience users
Allows the program to recover and continue executing
Provides meaningful feedback instead of a cryptic stack trace
Enables logging for debugging and monitoring
Protects data integrity — failed operations can be rolled back
Improves security by not leaking internal details to end users

data.title: Common Runtime Errors in C#
data.content: These are real examples of errors you will encounter frequently. Each one has a specific exception type you can catch.

data.text: Older languages often used **return codes** to signal errors — for example, a function might return `-1` on failure and `0` on success. This approach has serious problems: return codes are easy to ignore, they mix error data with normal return values, and they don't naturally propagate up the call stack.

cards.title: Return Codes
cards.description: Functions return a special value to indicate failure

cards.title: Exceptions
cards.description: Errors are thrown as objects and propagate automatically
pros: Carry rich error details (message, stack trace)
Propagate up the call stack automatically
Separate error handling from main logic

data.title: Best Practice: Fail Fast
data.text: Detect errors as early as possible. Validate arguments at the start of a method using guard clauses. This makes bugs easier to find because the failure happens close to its source, not deep in another method.

data.title: Exception Handling Layers
items: At the source — fix the underlying bug so the exception never occurs
Near the boundary — catch exceptions at API boundaries (UI layer, HTTP endpoint)
At the top level — a global exception handler for truly unexpected errors
Never swallow exceptions silently — always log or re-throw

terms.definition: An object representing an error that occurred during program execution, containing a message, stack trace, and optional inner exception.
Creating an exception object and signaling the runtime that an error has occurred using the `throw` keyword.
Intercepting an exception with a `catch` block to handle it before it terminates the program.
The process of an exception traveling up the call stack from the method that threw it until a catch block handles it.
A snapshot of the call stack at the moment an exception was thrown, showing the sequence of method calls that led to the error.
A pattern where a method checks its arguments for invalid values at the very beginning and throws immediately if something is wrong.

items.question: Will using try/catch make my code slower?
items.answer: No. In C#, the cost of having a try/catch block is essentially zero when no exception is thrown. The runtime only allocates the exception object and performs the stack walk when an exception actually occurs.

items.question: Should I use exceptions for normal program flow?
items.answer: No. Exceptions are for exceptional situations — errors that should not happen during normal operation. Do not use exceptions to control regular logic like checking if a file exists before reading it.

items.question: What is the difference between an error and an exception?
items.answer: In C#, 'error' is a general term for anything that goes wrong, while an 'exception' is the specific object the runtime creates and throws when that error occurs.

items.question: Can I catch all exceptions with one catch block?
items.answer: Yes, using `catch (Exception ex)`. However, you should only use this as a safety net after specific catch blocks. Catching Exception blindly can hide bugs you should fix.

data.title: Lesson Summary
points: An exception is an object representing a runtime error with message, stack trace, and inner exception details
Exceptions bubble up the call stack until a matching catch block handles them
C# exceptions are better than return codes because they carry rich details and propagate automatically
Common exceptions include NullReferenceException, FormatException, and IndexOutOfRangeException
Handle exceptions near boundaries — the UI layer or API entry points
Never let exceptions go unhandled in production; always log or display a meaningful message
Guard clauses validate arguments at the start of a method to fail fast
data.takeaway: Error handling is not an afterthought — it is a fundamental part of writing software that users can trust.
